Its range lies in the middle and high frequencies, its pitch is comparatively high, and it stands out clearly in an ensemble. Because the nylon head can be tuned, the player can adjust the pitch and get a warm, springy sound. The conical body helps it resonate naturally and gives the sound depth. Compared with the heaviness of a conventional drum kit, the timbal is lighter and more mobile; compared with the conga its tone is brighter and cleaner, with plenty of rhythm. The instrument suits Afro-Brazilian rhythms especially well and can set a hot, high-spirited mood.

The timbal (also called the timbau) is a membranophone derived from the caxambu drum, common in Bahia, Brazil, and originating in Salvador. The body is slightly conical and comes in various sizes; it is usually light, made of lacquered wood or metal (mostly aluminium), with an adjustable nylon head, and it looks like an ice-cream cone with the top and the tip cut off. It is mostly played with both hands, in a manner similar to the atabaque. It is used mainly for Afro-Brazilian rhythms such as axé and samba-reggae; in the 1980s a musical and social movement carried it into popular music.

It is also often played as a hand drum in the manner of the atabaque, which is used in Candomblé rites, so you can hear it both in ritual rhythms and in pop line-ups. It is used mostly for Afro-Brazilian rhythms such as axé and samba-reggae. It is played in a manner similar to the atabaque, a version of which came to Brazil with slavery and is used in Candomblé rites. In the 1980s a musical and social movement pushed the timbal into popular music.
